question: to the Commission François Kalfon (S&D) Subject:

Regulation (EU) 2022/2560 on foreign subsidies (FSR)1, in force since 2023, fills a loophole under which subsidies from third countries were not subjected to any scrutiny while intra-EU state aid was. On 14 July 2026, the Commission published its review report, in which it declared the Regulation to be fit for purpose and announced adjustments to the procedural setup. On 31 July 2026, the Commission served a statement of objections on PDD Holdings and its subsidiary WhaleCo Technology (Temu) for obstructing an inspection conducted in Dublin in December 2025 by refusing to provide information on the organisation of its operations, IT systems and certain records. Under Article 17 of the FSR, such an infringement is punishable by a fine of up to 1 % of the group’s global turnover. 1.

Given that this company has consistently demonstrated its willingness to circumvent European law on digital matters, consumer protection and state aid, will the Commission confirm that it will fully apply the penalties provided for under the FSR if the alleged obstruction is proven?
Given that the FSR is due to be revised in the near future, will the Commission draw lessons from this case to tighten up compliance and penalty procedures?
ELI: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2022/2560/oj.
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (24.9.2026) Companies operating in the internal market are legally obliged to submit to an inspection ordered by a decision of the Commission pursuant to Article 14 of the Foreign Subsidies Regulation (FSR)1. In the present case, the Commission takes the preliminary view that Temu has obstructed the inspection conducted at its premises last December, by refusing to submit to the inspection and by not providing the required books or other records in a complete form. Should the investigation confirm those preliminary findings, the Commission may impose a fine of up to 1% of Temu’s aggregate turnover of the previous financial year. In accordance with Article 17(6) FSR, when setting the amount of a fine, the Commission has regard to the nature of the identified infringements, their gravity and duration, taking due account of the principles of proportionality and appropriateness. Compliance with FSR provisions and possible breaches are examined under the FSR, and separately from compliance with other EU or national legislations. In July 2026, the Commission published the results of its first review of the FSR, from which it found that the regulation is fit for purpose to address distortions in the internal market caused by foreign subsidies, while acknowledging certain concerns about complexity and administrative burden. The Commission is envisaging targeted adjustments to the FSR procedural framework2.
1 Regulation (EU) 2022/2560 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 14 December 2022 on foreign
subsidies distorting the internal market, OJ L 330, 23.12.2022, p. 1. 2 https://ec.europa.eu/commission/presscorner/detail/en/ip_26_1606.
